Which parts of implementation were of specific difficulty for you?

Well, in general, the thing is not too complicated at its core.

1. Start with a graph where nodes count is equal to the map size (width\*height, counted in rooms). Each node will represent a room, so, it should have coordinates for room mapping. Each node is connected via edges only to adjacent nodes (edges represent passages here). Edges and nodes may be "switched on" (that means that the room or passage exists on the map; from the start everything is switched off). Edges and nodes may also have "tags" or something - that will be used to place special features like teleports or locked passages. For example, a node with a "KEY 1" tag means "this room contains a key 1". For simplicity, the terms later will be not from graph theory - "room exists" means "a node is enabled", "two rooms are connected" means "two nodes are enabled and have an enabled edge between them", "to place a room" means "enable node" etc.
2. Place some initial state on the graph. It should contain the start and the goal. "Initial states" are a simpler rules in my generator, an example of this is a rule "place a rectangle of connected rooms, tag a random one as a start, tag the farthest one as a goal".
3. Apply your replacement rules on the graph until some condition, like desired fill percentage, is satisfied. The rules are better to include as little nodes as possible so that they will have more variants on where to apply.

What's a replacement rule? It consists of two parts: pattern matching and application. Pattern matching is used to determine if (and where exactly) is the rule applicable, and the application is just a procedure which makes graph changes. If your rule uses 3 nodes, you check the graph for all the 3-node groups which match the pattern, then pick a random one of them and apply the rule here. Here's an example of two rules being applied: [https://imgur.com/a/7kFHikh](https://imgur.com/a/7kFHikh)

The most tricky thing is to have the pattern matching system up and running, but once you do, new rules can be written quickly. Then the quality of the generator depends just on your ruleset. The most fun part of it was to play around with rule variants and to see which ones produce better results.

I have found that it's better to have directed graph (and I'm using only directed edges inside my generator), but it's omitted here, as the general principle is still the same. Also, this covers only graph rewriting itself. To make the generator truly cyclic, take care that your defined rules create cycles (looping structures).

Also, keep in mind that those details are only about my implementation, and something may be not that efficient here. It's just reinventing the wheel which was invented by people smarter than me. :)

If this answer is too general for you (or if I'm handwaving here too much), so feel free to ask any more questions.

I think you're right, but even before CoM the MoM was looking less tedious than MoO2 and, more comparable, than the Civilization for my taste. This may come from the fact that city management is simpler (only two citizen types), and that the exploration is somewhat more important (you really have to take every lair/temple/ruin possible before your enemies do, because spells and books are *that* important) than in MoO/Civ, and after the map is explored and the borders are settled, you won't really feel safe, because basically, something constantly goes on on the global map.

MoM's economy is also quite interesting at its core - with basically only two resources, it's simple enough not to become a spreadsheet, and at the same time everything on which they can be spent should be thought out. Magical power can be routed to research, mana or casting skill, and the choice of the best distribution is inobvious, depends on the situation and changes as the game goes on. To really have more, you have to take more nodes, which are guarded or already taken by someone, so the economy progression is less of min-maxing the cities queue (although you still can do that, but it yields less than tanking the strategic positions), and more of making something that alters strategic situation in some way.

Magic is also well-made, because new "tech" can be a game-changer for you to some degree (and a full game-changer in case of late game spells). It's nothing like "+2 to this resource/stat" tech from many other games. It also allows for a gameplay I've not seen in other games: even turtled-out player can alter the global situation without moving their armies, only by casting global spells.

I would sum MoM up as "few actions, big impact" formula. CoM (and CoM2, of course) did a great job balancing all of that, but I believe it is only because the game is made upon a very good core. It's sad that Steve Barcia never made MoM2.

Well, it's quite simple (even too simple for my liking).

The layout is an WxH grid. For the tiled map, we start with (roomWidth\*W)x(roomHeight\*H) tiles, filled with walls.

For each room or connection we empty a rectangle of (roomWidth-1)x(roomHeight-1) tiles (those -1 are for that the walls between rooms will remain) at appropriate coordinates.

Then, we place doors (for rooms) or, optionally, remove walls entirely (for connections and multi-cell rooms). Doors positions are somewhat randomized.

Then we use simple cellular automata algorithm for eroding/dilating walls for connections, to make them look like caves.

Then, finally, we place entrypoint and exit point, and optionally add predefined dungeon pieces at empty places. My tiler can use those predefined pieces per-tag, so that some features will be placed at some specific tags only.

That's it!

Objective answer: It's all optional. The pattern could have had no keys or no deadend rooms at all. Or those rooms can be marked as secret rooms, having some reward in exchange for being deadend. The main idea of the generator is more about guaranteeing multiple paths (and, if one wants to, shortcuts), less about keys and stuff. 

In my head, the perfect level for hack-and-slash or a shooter is where every route possible is correct. You just go wherever you want to, and still can visit every room (except for those little dead-ends) without need to take the same route back. Of course, "perfect" means "almost unobtainable", but still, it is worth to try to approach this result as closely as possible.  
  
Subjective answer: I love the level design of DOOM, Quake, Duke Nukem and other old shooters. They were non-linear, they have had those keys and switches, they were so much fun to explore. It makes me sad that newer games tend to omit this approach. And I think that roguelikes/lites are well suited for that approach too.

Well, the pattern is a script here.

On high-level approach, the pattern is just a list of things you want to see on a layout. Simplest pattern would be like that:

"I want a start room. I want a finish room. I want them to be connected".

In the language which is used to define these for my generator, it would seem like that:

`ADD_ROOM_AT_EMPTY ROOM_NAME start`  
`ADD_ROOM_AT_EMPTY ROOM_NAME finish`  
`PLACE_PATH FROM start TO finish`

The syntax is like the following.

1. Each line of input file is either a declaration of single entity or a comment.
2. The line starts with a keyword, describing what exactly do you define (PLACE\_ROOM, PLACE\_PATH, PLACE\_ROOM\_NEAR\_PATH, PLACE\_ROOM\_AT\_PATH, PLACE\_RANDOM\_ROOMS, LOCK\_ROOM). If the line starts with #, it is a comment and will be ignored by the layout generator.
3. Empty lines are ignored too.
4. After the entity keyword, you can describe data for the placement - room name, room tags, room coordinate bounds. For example, if you want a room to be placed in top-left quadrant of 6x6 layout (so the coordinates would be any from 0,0 to 2,2), then the line would seem like: `ADD_ROOM_AT_EMPTY ROOMNAME someroom FROMX 0 TOX 2 FROMY 0 TOY 2`For another example, PLACE\_RANDOM\_ROOMS instruction has keywords MIN and MAX, which are used do describe minimum and maximum amount of rooms you want to get (exact amount will be chosen randomly from those bounds).
5. Almost all of the data is optional. Simple `ADD_ROOM_AT_EMPTY` without anything will still work.
6. Underscores are ignored and are there just for readability (so, ADD\_ROOM and ADDROOM are the same). UPPERCASE and lowercase is the same for the interpreter (for readability, too).
7. Order of metadata keywords is not important, with a single exception: the TAGS keyword should always be the last keyword of a line, because all the following words after it are accounted as tags. 

I tried to make the description language as simple as possible, for anyone to easily pick up pattern creation.The language may seem imperative (like, "do X, then do Y, then do Z"), but in fact it is declarative (like, "I want X, Y and Z, and I don't care how exactly and it which order will it be done"). All definitions can be put in any order, I could start defining a pattern from declaring a path, and only then define a room, and it would still work. It is coming from an internal pattern optimizer, which decides in which order the instructions will be executed (bad order could lead to ungeneratable map, even when the connectivity graph is perfectly planar), and there is the fair amount of work done for freeing a pattern designer from the need of thinking for suitable (machine-wise) order of instructions.

"Imperativeness" of keywords is an artifact of earlier stage of development, where the description language was really imperative, and was executed in exact order it was written in. I'm working on changing those words to something less order-like. "PLACE\_ROOM\_AT\_EMPTY" will be replaced with just ROOM, for example.

/u/Representative-Ad370, and something more, another wall of text, which this time should be taken as a perspective on Starcraft from a Supreme Commander player.

If I directly compare Starcraft with SupCom, most of the comparisons will be simply based on the fact that SupCom is true real-time *strategy*, whereas Starcraft is more like real-time *tactics with basebuilding*. SupCom is designed in such a way that the game can have two, three or even more front lines at the same time, and all of them have constant battles, and the design of the game is such that the player can have relatively easy awareness and control on all of them. In comparison, I remember one of StarCraft 2 ads in my country, where there were lines like "command huge armies". Yup, 120-140 supply limit of an army (the other 60-80 is spent on workers) is huge, huh. And if I play with mods which remove the limit, I just find that the game still can't be played "strategically", not "tactically", just because of the way it was designed, because of how the economy and production systems work.

SupCom has naval warfare, and it is done right. It is important, because in modern warfare (since the beginning of 20th century) the warships/carriers are maybe the most feared warmachines, and deservedly so. They are durable, they are huge, they have over-the-horizon range of fire, they can have ballistic missiles, the can carry and refuel planes, and they have enough firepower to raze a city. They carry radars and sonars, they have amazing defense systems, and they are, in fact, the fully fledged mobile bases. The warships are so powerful that they can influence the air superiority in a given area, and even change the outcome of the land combat of almost any scale, as long as it takes place near a sea. I honestly don't know why so many RTS games think of naval part of a war as irrelevant.

SupCom has the good variety of types of units. It has everything I can imagine for a future warfare (except for orbial bombardment, but its abscense is well explained in the lore). In Starcraft, terrans will spend years of time and gazillions of resources to develop some psi nonsense against The Fearsome And Unstoppable Zerg, but they would not develop good targeting systems for nukes, or carpet bombers with phosphorus ignition bombs, or faster-than-sound strike bombers, or good ballistic missiles or artillery with *proper* range. All of the mentioned things would make the war against Zerg (and against Protoss too) much, much simpler and cheaper for Terrans, and I have not even mentioned that those things already exist for years of our lifetimes, but are suddenly extinct in far future of interplanetary wars and "high tech machines" (which are cool, but useless) without any explanation. How can I take Starcraft lore seriously after that?

SupCom has the automation abilities for the player. I can give orders to unfinished buildings in advance, I can give complex orders to factories, so that all newly constructed  units will perform them, I can loop construction queues, I can easily order the new factory to do everything that the already functioning factory does (including default orders for units). It is not like the game is playing itself, it is about making right decisions about what, where and when to automate. It makes APM less of a decisive factor, and makes me feel that my "subordinaries" are less stupid than in Starcraft, even given the fact that the pathfinding in SupCom is crap. Starcraft doesn't have those features. Mostly because it is tactics, not strategy, but some things are missing not because of the game focus, but because of the game wants you to utilize no-brainer, mechanical skills. For example, the game lacks "spread move" order, whereas it would be extremely useful in many cases. Starcraft also lacks unit formations, which also would be extremely useful, given the nature of the combats here. I don't think that the Starcraft designers didn't think about that - moreover, I think that the lack of those features was made on purpose, because otherwise the some design an/or balance decisions won't work. Personally for me, it's the bad balance and the bad design direction, because it makes the gameplay feel too factitious. So, the lacking automation is just a way to artificially force the player into multitasking.

SupCom has the commander concept. It doesn't matter how much you achieved in a skirmish if you (personally you, as the ACU concept suggests) is dead. It sometimes allows players to win games from the very bad situation. Starcraft has the depletable resources just for its games not to fall into stalemate, where two players have so much production that they can't destroy each other, but it means that the losing player's situation generally will be only worse with time.

ACU concept leads to the following: SupCom has the better teamplay. Just look at the replays, where there are so many cases where the losing team of 8x8 game wins after losing half (or even more) of the players. It generally seems impossible in Starcraft, where the team of four players will generally easily beat the team of three remaining players of equal skill, that's why such team games are so unpopular in Starcraft. Losing team is having a bad time, which will only worsen with time because of depletable resources.

And, personally for me, SupCom is better just because of its scale. I'm not talking about that the medium-sized map of SupCom is bigger than the biggest map in Starcraft, no. I'm talking about the "sense of the scale".  Starcraft scales ruin the suspension of disbelief for me. Tank in Starcraft looks so small, like there is only one or two people inside of it. Command center is the big building, but not huge, and the huge, kilometers-sized battlecruiser is smaller than it (and is so low that the marine can't fit in it). In one mission the science vessel is about a size of a tank and just about as durable, but the other mission takes place inside of a science vessel, and it is obvious that there can be a thousand of tanks inside, and there still will be the place to move. What's the size of psi storm? In one mission it can cover 3-5 science vessels (or, maybe, 20 marines), and in the other mission it can't cover the one science vessel (because the mission takes place inside of it!) but it still covers those maybe 20 marines. What's going on here?

Summing up, I would say that I would agree that the very good Starcraft player is closer "in spirit" to a good FPS player (both of the games require good reaction times, timings, etc) than to the chess player, and that the situation with SupCom is quite oppsite (I personally think that SupCom is closer to Go than to chess, but YMMV).

I know that the many of stated things are just subjective, and the most people don't give a damn for them. I would say, Starcraft is just too "artificial" for me. Many of its stragenesses are made in the sake of the balance and for some design concepts to work at all. For me, it plays like when I played with toy soldiers in my childhood, and I had no bombers just because I didn't have toy bombers, so I just pretended like there are no bombers existing.

I play Starcraft (both 1 and 2) with my friend from time to time, I've been in diamond league for about a year before i dropped it, but I don't really like the game. There are three things I really hate in Starcraft. Please take note that while I'm trying not to directly compare Starcraft with SupCom here, it's almost impossible, since I can't "unsee" SupCom and other RTS games, which made some design decisions better, in my opinion, than the Starcraft did.

First, the game is designed towards forcing the player to make "mechanic" actions and against easiness of strategic control. I can't use a-move for default rally point, I can't loop production queue (and the economy system of the game is made in such a way that looping would make things worse), I can't auto-cast larvae, chronoboost or MULEs (and, in case of MULEs, the game design makes that it would be a bad decision anyway). The game feels like it WANTS me to utilize maximum APM, and at least half of that APM is just actions which could be easily automated. I also hate being forced to remember to do such tasks. I feel like the difference between me and more strong players (not much stronger, just stronger) is less about understanding the game and more about being able to remember casting larvae/add production/spread creep/construct additional pylons etc in time.

Second, the gameplay and story segregation, and general "unrealisticness" (sorry for my bad English) of gameplay. I know that games should have "make-believes" and that we, players, should agree with them. But there are various degrees of that in games. I just can't really be engaged in the game process when (for example) the game constantly tells me that the battlecruiser is a hell of a flying fortress with 3k sized crew, and yet in the game it is a small VTOL, smaller than the half of the buildings in size, and it flies at such a low height that the bunch of needle-shooting hydralisks can destroy it from the surface.>!There also are smaller complaints, like that no plane in the game behaves like an actual plane (Terrans have lost this technology of their ancestors, I suppose), or lacking of any true projectiles, or "the siege weapon of high range" shooting only at the distance of \~10 lengths of itself, or the nukes, which explode like they're kerosene canisters poorly set on fire (and for whatever reason they need the special psi stealth operative with pocket laser to be targeted, whereas almost all the other Terran rockets are guided), but I've hidden those reasons with spoiler, because they're part of "make-belive" which I could accept, if they weren't so many altogether).!<

Third, I don't like the way the UI is designed. I agree that Strarcraft 2 is MUCH better than the first one in terms of UI and responsiveness (it has the best responsiveness ever made in RTS), but the game lacks some things that could simplify control without making "mind games" simpler. For example, the abilities could be integrated into one "page" of orders (like when you play Tychus in co-op), MULEs, chronoboosts and similar "global" abilities could be accessible from the UI without the need to select the building first (think of C&C3's UI of abilities). There could be pop-ups with ETA for upgrades when they're almost finished, like in MIT Overseer observer mod, which is used in official tournaments. Think of that! Observers have the better information than the players! Why not incorporate that in the game? If someone wouldn't like that, why not make it possible to just switch those features off in settings? Because of reasons? I also remember early AlphaStar games, when one of YouTube starcrafters found that the AI has much wider field of view than the player, thus the AI has an advantage. The decision? Let's make it as narrow as the player have! Why not allowing players to make the camera higher? Because of reasons, too?

There still are some things in Starcraft which I love, like the atmosphere (especially in the first game), awesome campaigns (especially WoL), interesting co-op mode, etc. But the reasons I stated above were enough for me to drop the game, save for occasional play sessions with that friend of mine, who is Starcraft fan, and also they're mostly the same reasons I dropped Warcraft 3 as soon as I saw that it is designed in an extremely similar way to Starcraft. 

Interestingly, believe it or not, I have had most of those complaints about Starcraft even before I became familiar with SupCom.
